title: Common DNS Operational and Configuration Errors
summary: Describes errors often found in the way DNS servers are operated and configured, and in the data they contain. It is a practical checklist of mistakes to avoid. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a list of common mistakes people make when running the Internet's phone book, so others can avoid them.

can a cname coexist with other dns records
subtitle: A practical checklist of the mistakes people most often make in DNS zone data and in running nameservers.

tldr.problem: Running a nameserver is not trivial. Many things can go wrong, both in the data the servers hold and in how the servers are run, and the mistakes cause lost services and bounced mail.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through common errors in zone data (PTR and A records, SOA timers, glue, CNAME, MX, wildcards, delegation) and in BIND operation (serial numbers, zone file style, verification), and says what to do instead.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It summarizes current requirements and common practice as of 1996 and replaces RFC 1537.

today: RFC 1912 is an Informational memo from February 1996 that obsoletes RFC 1537. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its advice reflects 1996 practice and BIND versions, and it says security issues are not discussed in the memo.

sections.title: Why DNS Needs Care
sections.content:
RFC 1912 starts from a plain observation: running a nameserver is not a trivial task. Many decisions have to be made about what data to put in the DNS and how to set up servers, and many things can go wrong.

The memo covers two areas. Section 2 is about the data in the zone files that a nameserver loads. Section 3 is about operating the nameserver, specifically BIND. It also touches on resolver and server bugs and a few political issues. It tries to summarize current Internet requirements and common practice, and to expand on issues raised in RFC 1537.
sections.plainLanguage: Running a phone book for the whole Internet is harder than it looks. This memo lists the slips people make so you can dodge them.

sections.title: Names, PTR Records and Bad Data
sections.content:
Every Internet-reachable host should have a name, because many services will not talk to you if you are not correctly registered in the DNS. Make sure your PTR and A records match: every IP address, including every address of a multi-homed host, should have a matching PTR record in the in-addr.arpa domain, and a PTR must point back to a valid A record, not to a CNAME alias. The memo recommends software that automates this check.

Names used for hosts should follow host-name rules: only ASCII letters, digits and the hyphen character, with labels beginning and ending with a letter or digit and not made only of digits. Names used for mail follow the more liberal rules of RFC 822. The memo warns that underscores are risky, and that a name like 0xe can be read by the inet_ntoa() library call as an IP address.

Resource records such as HINFO and RP take more than one argument. If you do not supply enough, servers sometimes return garbage for the missing fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer needs a name in the phone book, and the name and the number must point at each other. Otherwise some places will not let you in.

sections.title: SOA Records and Timers
sections.content:
The SOA record of every zone must carry an e-mail address for the person who maintains the DNS, with the @ replaced by a .. The preferred choice is the generic name hostmaster, redirected by a mail alias. That address must reach real people, because it is used for everything from reporting bad DNS data to reporting security incidents.

Do not use decimal serial numbers. The recommended syntax is YYYYMMDDnn (year, month, day, revision number). A decimal serial can be incremented and still end up numerically lower after BIND converts it internally.

The four timers are given in seconds in the zone data. Refresh is how often a secondary polls the primary. Retry is the wait after a failed refresh. Expire is how long a secondary keeps serving when it cannot reach the primary. Minimum is the default TTL and is called by far the most important timer. The memo recommends values of 3 or more days for Minimum once a DNS has stabilized, and turning it down temporarily before major changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The timers tell helper servers how often to check for news and how long old news is still good. Too short wastes effort, and too long keeps stale answers around.

sections.title: Glue, CNAME, MX and Wildcard Records
sections.content:
Glue records are A records attached to NS records to provide bootstrapping information. They are needed only in forward zone files, for nameservers located in the subdomain being delegated. Adding a glue record whenever you add an NS record, just to make sure, is a bad habit: stale duplicates are hard to track down when a server moves.

A CNAME must not coexist with any other data. Putting a CNAME beside the NS records of a domain, as a way to make the domain also a host, makes servers like BIND ignore the NS entries. Do not point MX, CNAME, PTR or NS records at a CNAME. Aliases are encouraged for generalized names such as ftp and www.

The memo advises giving every host an MX record, even if it points to itself. A wildcard MX applies only to names not listed in the DNS at all, so it is not a way to cover every host. It can also make operations succeed that should fail, such as mail to a misspelled host. WKS records are deprecated by RFC 1123, and HINFO should hold only machine information, with TXT for anything else.
sections.plainLanguage: Some entries in the phone book cannot sit next to each other. An alias is like a forwarding sign, so you cannot also put a different answer on the same line.

sections.title: Delegation Errors and Lame Servers
sections.content:
You are required to have at least two nameservers for every domain, with secondaries outside your own network. A lame delegation exists when a nameserver is named in NS records for a zone but is not actually providing nameservice for it. At best it causes extra DNS traffic. At worst you get unresolved hosts and bounced e-mail.

When a nameserver is moved or removed, cached NS records keep pointing at it. To avoid lame delegations while caches age out, keep providing nameservice on the old server for the length of the maximum of the minimum plus refresh times for the zone and the parent zone.

Make sure the parent domain lists the same NS records as you do. Do not list too many: 7 is the recommended maximum. Too many risks overflowing the 512-byte limit of a UDP response, after which resolvers fall back to TCP and load on your nameserver rises.
sections.plainLanguage: A lame delegation is a phone book that says to ask a certain person, but that person has no idea. Always check that the person you list really knows the answer.

sections.title: Running BIND Day to Day
sections.content:
Each zone has a serial number, and a secondary asks for new data only if the primary's serial is greater. So you must change the serial whenever you change the data. If you set it too high by mistake, the memo gives a multi-step procedure: add 2147483647 to the incorrect number, subtract 4294967296 if the result exceeds that, load it, wait two refresh periods, and repeat until you can set the target. It does not work if a secondary runs BIND 4.8.3 or earlier.

For zone files, be consistent: use fully qualified names everywhere, or unqualified names everywhere. Always remember the trailing dot on a fully qualified name, because without it the server appends $ORIGIN. After each change, verify with dig or a similar tool, check syslog on reload, and automate the checking where you can.

Certain zones should always be present: localhost, 0.0.127.in-addr.arpa, 255.in-addr.arpa and 0.in-addr.arpa. The memo also strongly encourages turning on UDP checksums on systems that disable them.
sections.plainLanguage: Whenever you change the phone book, you must also change its edition number, or the other copies will never update. Then check your work before you walk away.
